newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HONG KONG EXCHANGE FUND TO SEE HARSH 1997 - HKMA.
newsitem.headline: HONG KONG EXCHANGE FUND TO SEE HARSH 1997 - HKMA.

text.p: Hong Kong boasts one of the world's highest foreign reserves but its Exchange Fund will see a harsh 1997 with expected U.S. interest rate rises, a firm U.S. dollar and poor bond markets, the central bank said on Thursday.
"The (Fund's) outlook for 1997 remains uncertain," Andrew Sheng, deputy chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the de facto central bank, told a news conference.

"Market consensus that U.S. interest rates may increase in 1997, coupled with the strength in the U.S. dollar will impact on the Fund's performance in 1997," he said. "World bond markets have proved very difficult so far this year."
"It is likely that 1997 will be a more difficult year than 1996 for a portfolio principally dominated by bonds such as the Exchange Fund," he added.
The Exchange Fund, which now covers 6.5 times of bank notes in issue in the territory, is used to back the Hong Kong dollar.
The HKMA said foreign reserves held in the Exchange Fund, excluding unsettled forward transactions, stood at US$63.8 billion -- the world's seventh largest -- at the end of February.
That represents a drop from the US$65.9 billion post at the end of January. Sheng attributed the decline to seasonal factors.
Total assets of the Exchange Fund stood at HK$534.5 billion at the end of 1996, up 16 percent year on year, the HKMA said.
Sheng said the modest increase was due to slower growth in note circulation, a rise in fiscal reserves account and an increase in Exchange Fund bills and notes.
Of the total assets, HK$493.8 billion was in foreign currency assets and HK$40.72 billion in Hong Kong dollar assets.

Sheng said the HKMA had raised the weighting of U.S. dollar assets to 88 percent of the total assets as at the end of 1996, from 84 percent a year earlier. That adjustment was made at the expense of the weightings of assets in Japanese and European currencies.
The U.S. dollar firmed seven percent against the mark and 12 percent against the yen in 1996, he noted.

"U.S. dollar will always be the major element of the Fund due to our currency link. Almost all interest-bearing liabilities are hedged into U.S. dollars," he said. Hong Kong dollar is pegged at HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar.
European currencies' weighting in the Fund was bigger than the yen's, Sheng said, without giving figures.
He noted European currencies might become more volatile this year, while uncertainties also clouded European markets.
Accumulated earnings in the Exchange Fund grew 7.9 percent to HK$172.8 billion at the end of 1996.
Sheng attributed the earnings rise, in a year dogged by volatile bond markets and a strong U.S. dollar, partly to investment in U.S. equities which rallied strongly in 1996.
Amy Yip, HKMA's executive director (reserves management), said equity investment, mostly in U.S. stocks, amounted to five percent of the Fund last year.

She said despite the prospect of U.S. interest rate rises the HKMA had no present intention to reduce the weighting of U.S. stocks in the Fund this year because stock investment should take a long-term view.
The Fund's investment income fell to HK$25.38 billion last year from HK$46.73 billion in 1995. Sheng said the fall was due to U.S. bond price falls and a firm U.S. dollar in 1996.
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6590
